options: An empty string
The number zero
An unknown or not-applicable value — the absence of a value entirely

questions.explain: NULL is not zero, not empty text — it means the value is unknown or doesn't apply.

questions.q: Why does 'WHERE MiddleName = NULL' return zero rows, even when NULLs exist?
options: It's a syntax error that SQL Server silently ignores
= NULL only works with numeric columns
MiddleName can never actually be NULL in SQL Server
An unknown value can't be said to equal anything, so = NULL always evaluates to unknown/false
questions.explain: This is a classic beginner trap — equality comparisons against NULL never evaluate to true, regardless of the data.

questions.q: What is the correct way to test for NULL?
options: == NULL
IS NULL / IS NOT NULL
LIKE NULL
= NULL / <> NULL
questions.explain: IS NULL and IS NOT NULL are special syntax built specifically for this purpose, not regular comparison operators.

options: Deletes rows where MiddleName is NULL
Returns MiddleName's value if it's not NULL, otherwise returns '(none)'
Tests whether MiddleName is NULL, returning true or false
Converts every value to '(none)' regardless of MiddleName
questions.explain: ISNULL substitutes a default value only when the first argument is NULL.

questions.q: How does COALESCE() differ from ISNULL()?
options: COALESCE only works with text columns
COALESCE accepts any number of arguments and returns the first non-NULL one; ISNULL takes exactly two
ISNULL is the ANSI-standard version; COALESCE is SQL Server-specific
They are functionally identical in every respect
questions.explain: COALESCE(a, b, c, ...) can chain multiple fallbacks; ISNULL is limited to exactly one replacement value. COALESCE is also the ANSI-standard function.
